Method

Use it when you want to know which defect kinds were checked where.

Terms on this page

Evidence
A pointer to code at a commit (file, symbol, lines) with a note of how strong it is: read in code, seen in a test, stated in a comment, and so on.
Concern
One kind of defect worth looking for in this codebase, such as a race on a shared cache. The review checklist is the full list.
Concern review
The verdict for one concern in one subsystem: bug found, acceptable, ruled out, out of scope, or undecided.

§Concern reasoning

Why each subsystem's concerns apply where they do, in the survey's words.

§R-02 — Survey ladder and judgment records

§concern CR-1

The concern was framed as: does any gate in this subsystem check the record in one step and write in another, such that a second server process can change the record in between? Three writers do. update_subsystem_status reads the status (mcp-server/src/tools/subsystems.ts:update_subsystem_status@ec39380 lines 219-236) and runs enforceForwardPrerequisites and requireExplanationDischarge, then opens a separate transaction for the UPDATE and the ladder row (lines 248-260). upsert_subsystem has the same shape. set_disposition checks depth with requireSubsystemStatus before its transaction (mcp-server/src/tools/dispositions.ts:set_disposition@ec39380 lines 98-99, 187-228). define_term also reads the existing row outside its transaction, but the interleaving there is harmless: each write inserts its own subsystem into vocabulary_scopes, so neither subsystem loses its discharge.

Compensating mechanisms considered: better-sqlite3 runs a process's calls one at a time, which rules out interleaving inside one process but not between processes. db.ts opens its only immediate transaction when the store is first opened (line 126), and rg finds no lock or busy timeout that serializes tool writes. The skill tells a coordinator to acquire_lock on the subsystem id before each phase, but that lock is advisory and no R-02 writer consults it. The verdict is confirmed-bug with severity LOW: the window needs two sessions working the same subsystem at once, with one of them resetting it. The evidence is code-verified. The linchpin flag is off because all four context dimensions were read: the call paths, the comments that explain the one-transaction design, the supported shared-store configurations, and the scope across all three status writers.

Recorded 2026-11-24 at ec393801.

§P-02 — Store schema, migrations and storage history

§Several processes, one store: concern CR-1, concern AT-1, concern TB-2

All three concerns turn on the same fact: inside one server process every call here is synchronous (better-sqlite3 and spawnSync), so the only interleavings are with another process holding the same memory.db.

  • concern CR-1 was framed as "which read-then-write sequence spans more than one SQLite statement with no lock held". The invariants predicates do (the standing check issues about eight reads with git calls between), but they read before their caller's write, and R-02's R02-2 already records that check-then-write gap on the status ladder. The sequence that is P-02's own is the migration probe: mcp-server/src/db.ts:hasColumn@ec39380 then an ALTER, each autocommit. Two first-time openers of a pre-upgrade store can both probe false; the second ALTER is refused by SQLite as a duplicate column and its open throws. Nothing else serialises opens: index.ts opens lazily with no lock and project.ts ensureProjectStorage takes none for an existing store. Graded LOW because the window is one open per upgrade and the cost is one failed call, and linchpin because SQLite's duplicate-column refusal is runtime behaviour, not code read here.
  • concern AT-1 was framed as "what does a phase gate commit when another process writes between the checkpoint and git". Rows written after the TRUNCATE checkpoint stay in the untracked WAL and reach the next gate, which is acceptable for a recovery point. What remains unexamined is git reading memory.db while another process's checkpoint writes into it; no lock covers that, and no test injects it. Kept acceptable and linchpin rather than a bug because a just-truncated WAL makes a second checkpoint in that window unlikely, and that likelihood is an inference.
  • concern TB-2: the repository sets no busy_timeout on memory.db; the bound is better-sqlite3's constructor default of 5000 ms, read in the installed package, which is not a tracked path, so the disposition is linchpin on a dependency default. The checkpoint itself refuses a busy result rather than hanging.

Recorded 2026-11-24 at ec393801.

§R-01 — Survey scope, ledger and reconciliation

§Concern reasoning

The concerns that start in R-01 are concern AT-2, concern CC-2, concern SI-2 and concern IF-3. concern AT-2 holds: detect_changes reads every store row its digests describe inside the BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction that inserts the reading, and the only reads before it are git's answers about an immutable commit.

concern CC-2 holds in the sense that matters. Every write that changes what a reconciliation counts (a ledger path or classification, a rule, a sorting row, a retirement of an active row) moves an input of a digest; the writes that move none (clear_staleness, a re-add that changes only ref_sha or why_in_scope, the scope inventory) change nothing the reconciliation counted. The tests prove this mostly through raw SQL rather than through each tool.

concern SI-2 holds: precedence and tie-break are written once, in scope.ts, and the completion checker does not decide membership itself; it reads the recorded exclusions and restates only the pattern grammar to find uncovered paths.

concern IF-3 fails in one case. Staleness is derived from each row's own ref_sha, so drift agrees across one or two reconciliations, but a row marked absent is never re-derived: markStale skips already stale rows and markFresh skips absent ones. A file deleted and restored between reconciliations therefore stays absent, clear_staleness refuses it with advice that does not help, and only retire-and-re-add clears it (finding R01-1).

Of the concerns seeded elsewhere, concern CR-1 is latent here: update_file_classification, clear_staleness and retire_ledger_file read before they write in separate statements, which matters only with two server processes on one store. concern TB-1 and concern TB-2 hold through the subprocess wrapper's 120 s limit, though detect_changes holds the write lock across its git diffs. concern TR-1, concern TR-3, concern AO-1, concern RL-2, concern CC-3 and concern EP-1 hold on the code cited. The remaining nineteen concerns are about code other subsystems own.

Recorded 2026-11-24 at ec393801.

§P-01 — Server runtime and dispatch

§Concern reasoning

The concerns that start in P-01 are concern TB-1, concern AO-1, concern EP-1, concern CR-1, concern TR-1 and concern TR-3.

concern CR-1 fails at the place the probe names: acquire_lock checks for a holder and then upserts in separate statements, and the upsert overwrites any holder, so two processes can both be granted one lock (P01-1). Within one process the dispatcher runs synchronous handlers one at a time, so the race needs two processes.

concern TR-1 fails at the path guard: one leading ./ is stripped and . segments are not refused, so ././.amanuensis/x passes the reservation of tool state; the scope guard then cannot canonicalize that spelling and judges the raw one, which is why concern SI-2 fails too (P01-2). The same fallback means a path written with . segments or doubled slashes is recorded under a different name from its canonical one. A caller's revision reaches git rev-parse without --end-of-options, which is hardening debt rather than a demonstrated flaw.

concern TB-1 holds: the wrapper bounds every call made through it, and the direct child_process calls in index.ts, orientation-lint.ts and git-blobs.ts carry their own limits; the guarantee depends on the startup-bounds scan, since the other scan misses async spawn. concern AO-1 holds: the shared state is the process context, an eight-entry cache of immutable commit trees and the call-log queue. concern EP-1 is delegated: the dispatcher rolls nothing back, so atomicity is judged in each handler's subsystem; P-01's own handlers write one row or a harmless pair. concern TR-3 holds for P-01's SQL, but the repository's identifier checker validates only table names and passes when it finds nothing. concern TB-2, concern CR-3 and concern RL-3 hold for the call-log sidecar.

§R-03 — Evidence, claims and findings

§Concern reasoning

Ten of the thirty-three concerns touch R-03's own code; the rest belong to the store, the index, the materializer, publishing or installation, and R-03 only reads or relies on them.

Concurrency was the first question, because several servers can share a store. The answer differs by record. For claims the database carries the rule: a partial unique index allows one open version per key, and the immutability trigger lets a version be closed exactly once, so a second invalidation from another process aborts even though invalidate_claim's UPDATE is unconditional. For findings only the severity re-grade takes BEGIN IMMEDIATE. update_finding_status and verify_finding_fix read state before writing, and duplicate-mark and withdraw-once are read-then-insert with no unique index. These interleavings can produce a stale rationale, a duplicate event or a duplicate mark, but no lost or contradictory record, so concern CR-1 is acceptable. That judgement is inferred; no test runs two processes.

Partial writes are not a risk here: every multi-row writer is one transaction, and git and the code index run before it opens. Symbol identity is per revision: an anchor stores the definition's symbol_id, blob and span hash at ref_sha, and a hash mismatch degrades to an unanchored row. Git receives the caller's revision without an end-of-options marker, but probing showed git rev-parse --verify refuses option-shaped strings. SQL identifiers come from fixed lists or the generated vocabulary.

The defect this pass found is not one of the seeded concerns. The overturn gate checks that some evidence was attached in this session. It does not check that the evidence disproves anything, and there is no role that could say so. A survey session that records a finding with its symptom evidence can therefore rule it out with no further evidence (R03-1).

§C-01 — Locus route, standing and attention

§Concern reasoning

C-01 writes nothing. The concerns that matter are about reading: whether a reader selects the effective row the way its writer defines it, and whether it says more than the record supports.

Cache coherence (concern CC-3) is where both findings sit. Claims and findings are selected correctly: an open interval, or ancestry under as_of_sha, and finding_state_current. get_history reads resolution events at fix_sha, but R-03 stores the revision an event belongs to in effective_sha, and describe_locus reads it from there (C01-1). describe_locus's terms section matches a path with an unescaped LIKE, so _ and % act as wildcards (C01-2).

Some helpers omit the active-ledger-row filter that the subsystem counts apply. That would let rows on excluded paths reach a reader, but this store has none, so it is latent. get_dashboard never claims a reconciliation stands, which is why concern CC-2 is acceptable; its unclassified count is a snapshot, not coverage.

Concurrency, time bounds, trust and identity concerns are acceptable. No read-then-write exists. Git runs through the bounded wrapper. An option-shaped as_of_sha is refused by git. Symbol matching prefers exact ids. Scope failure fails open on this read surface while the write guards refuse.

The tests are mostly strong on budgets and standing. Several checks accept any refusal or match source text, and none runs two processes.

§M-01 — Materializer entry, read model and publication

§concern TB-1 and the bound on the render

concern TB-1 asks whether every child process runs with a time limit. The python3 spawn does: materialize.ts:execute@ec393801 passes its own 900 s timeout, which subprocess.ts:bounded@ec393801 leaves alone, and chooses SIGTERM rather than the wrapper's SIGKILL so a clean publish stopped between its renames can restore the old output. The render's own git calls carry timeouts: 3 s for the origin URL (core.py:_repository_web_url@731918eb), 5 s for each remote-ref query (_repository_web_ref) and 10 s for the linked branch's tree (_remote_tree_paths), and each treats a timeout as no answer. The defect is in how the limit is enforced, not whether it is set: materialize.py:Terminated@ec393801 subclasses Exception, and the one broad handler in the package, the per-page build loop in core.py:Materializer._materialize@ec393801, catches Exception. A SIGTERM arriving while models are built becomes a page warning, the loop continues, and the process exits only when the render finishes. spawnSync sends its kill signal once and does not return until the child exits, so the server is held for the remainder; when it returns, result.error carries the timeout and execute reports it as a failure to start. Clean publish still fails closed (ok is false, the stage is deleted), which is why the finding is LOW. Quality is code-verified for every link except spawnSync's wait-until-exit, which is Node's documented behaviour and not in the tree.

concern SE-2 was framed through M-01's own contract rather than the skill's quotations: the tool descriptions are what an agent reads before calling. Both name Markdown; manifest.py writes views ['html'] and removes Markdown pages; the skill states no Markdown page is written. That is a contract contradiction with code-verified evidence on both sides.

concern CR-2 is confirmed-acceptable but linchpin-dependent. There is no explicit BEGIN in db.py:open_ro@ec393801, so in principle a page could mix records from before and after a write. Two things bound it: the calling server process cannot write while spawnSync blocks it, and the read-back re-reads the store after the pages are written. How completely the read-back compares a page with the store is M-05's, so the acceptability rests on a subsystem not yet read.

§P-03 — Workspace binding, activation and installer

§Concern reasoning

The concerns that bear on P-03 are the ones its seeding named: the temporal bound on startup probes, first-use atomicity, worktree identity, trust in environment and paths, and the installer's exceptional path and backups.

Store creation holds up. The stage-then-rename design means a store at the store path was either published whole or pre-dates the marker contract, and the recovery test exercises all twelve interruption boundaries. The residual risk is in reclaiming abandoned stages, which trusts a local pid probe. On a storage root shared between machines, another host's live stage would look abandoned. Nothing tests that deployment.

The probe bound is applied everywhere a child process runs, so nothing hangs. But the bound's own comment promises that an expired probe degrades to a fallback, and that is not true of the git origin probe. Its fallback is a different repository identity, and two exact-match checks refuse it: one on every tool call, one on every store adoption. So a slow git turns into a refusal that names an identity change, and a store created during such a window records the wrong identity for good.

The installer's per-file writes are sound: backup, temporary file, rename. What fails the probes is what lies between files. A host sequence that throws partway reports no partial result, and backups pile up beside the user's configuration without being named on a real run. Separately, the user-scope init path checks every directory against the Codex home, so it refuses the two other hosts it accepts as arguments.

About two thirds of the active concerns name machinery P-03 does not hold: the code index, reconciliation, the materializer's snapshot and escaping, schema migration, and vocabulary parity. P-03 hands those subsystems either a path or a context, and nothing more.

Recorded 2026-11-24 at ec393801.

§P-04 — Code index

§Concern reasoning

Two concerns are confirmed bugs, both LOW.

Concurrency across server processes is mostly handled by making each write one immediate transaction that re-checks what it depends on: publishing a blob skips one already published, and the completion marker is written only after every supported entry of the revision is found inside the same transaction. Eviction breaks the pattern. It reads its victims (blobs not referenced by the eight most recently touched trees) once, then deletes them in batches, each its own transaction, without asking again whether a kept tree now references them. A process that records and completes a newer tree in between keeps a completion marker for a tree whose blobs are gone, and find_symbol then answers that revision as complete while rows are missing (P04-1).

The wasm lifecycle is right on the common path: each Tree is deleted in a finally, and Parsers and Queries are loaded once per language and cached. The failure path is not. The tree-sitter runtime promise is cached even when it rejects, so one failed start disables parsing for the process; and if compiling a query throws, the Parser and Language just made are never deleted while the failed load is dropped from the cache, so every retry leaks another pair (P04-2).

The rest holds with residuals. A generation id covers grammars and queries by hash but covers extraction code only through a version constant someone must bump. Every one-shot git call is bounded through subprocess.ts and the batch reader carries its own per-read and lifetime kill timers; the maintainer scripts that fetch grammars run npm and tar unbounded. The sidecar sets a busy timeout and turns any non-corruption database error into an unavailable answer. Its one connection is closed on inode change, failed open and recovery. Corrupt files set aside by recovery are never removed. Paths are validated before use and git ls-tree takes them after a double dash; search text reaches SQL only as bound, quoted parameters, and the table names interpolated in eviction come from a fixed list. Rows are keyed by blob and language with a full tree per revision, so there is no incremental state to drift from a fresh build.

Concerns about publication, installation, store initialization, store schema and migrations, prose lint and shared vocabularies do not reach this subsystem.

Recorded 2026-11-24 at ec393801.

§M-05 — Publication read-back

§Concern reasoning

The concerns that reach the read-back are the publication's exceptional paths, its reading of a store that may be changing, its child processes, and its agreement with the server on what is current.

Exceptional paths mostly hold. Every condition the read-back detects becomes a mismatch on an axis and turns ok false, and a missing receipt is red everywhere. Two inputs escape that net: the tree listing decodes git's output strictly, so a tracked path that is not valid UTF-8 raises instead of reading as git not answering (as git_paths beside it already does), and a non-numeric badge count raises in the badge census. Either aborts verify with no summary (M05-1). That fails closed but leaves a repository with such a path unable to publish, with only a traceback to say why.

Some checks are weaker than their axis promises (M05-2). The coverage cell on About this survey passes on an unreconciled store if it contains the words not measured anywhere, even beside a number; an explanation or narrative line passes if its words occur anywhere on the page; a runtime boundary's four fields are owed separately, so two boundaries with swapped mechanisms pass. The receipt hash would catch a later edit, but not a renderer that misplaces text, which is what these checks are for.

The rest is acceptable. One read-only connection serves every census and is closed in a finally. The first census reads in autocommit; the first survey filter writes a TEMP table without committing, so the later censuses share one implicit transaction. Either way the store is read after the render, so a concurrent server write appears as a mismatch and fails closed. Every git call has a 30-second timeout and a timeout means the reconciliation does not stand. Optional tables and columns are guarded, effective rows are chosen as the server chooses them, and every digest a reconciliation depends on is re-derived before its counts are trusted. SQL is built only from fixed fragments.

Other concerns belong to the server, the renderers or the installer; the read-back reads lint.py and the generated vocabulary as the renderer does and leaves their agreement with the server to the subsystems that own them.

§R-04 — Explanations, narratives and project records

§Concern reasoning

Two seeded concerns turned up defects here, both low. The write path lints prose with the same Python orientation rule the pages use, but the overview also withholds a project purpose that carries a percentage, and no writer runs that second rule, so such a purpose is accepted and then withheld (R04-1, concern SE-3). register_artifact catches the path resolver's refusal and stores an escaping path with a null hash, and its upsert keeps a stale hash when the file later cannot be read (R04-2, concern TR-1); rehash and import still honour the resolver, so no file outside the store is read.

Six concerns hold as designed. Refusals come before the first write, and each multi-row write runs in one transaction (concern EP-1). Records are append-only with the newest row effective, so two interleaved writers only produce a later row (concern CR-1). The readers apply the same selection rule the Python read-back does, and a shared cases file runs both (concern CC-3). The lint child is bounded at thirty seconds and lets the write through on timeout (concern TB-1). SQL interpolates only a placeholder list (concern TR-3), evidence passes the shared survey-scope guard (concern SI-2), and module-scope values are constant tables (concern AO-1).

The rest are out of scope: R-04 opens no connection, sidecar, temporary directory or tree-sitter object, writes no ledger or scope row, and publishes nothing.

§R-05 — Vocabulary contract and parity checks

§Concern reasoning

Two concerns bear directly on R-05.

concern SE-4, whether the shared vocabularies can drift, holds. Both runtime copies are generated whole from one contract. --check fails on any byte difference, and the value lists are read back a second way as text. The contract itself refuses an evidence-quality list that is out of step with the evidence-kind list. CI runs all three.

concern SE-2, what the skill checks actually enforce, is where both findings sit. The headers are candid that the checks are string identity: names, not values, meanings or required arguments. Two weaknesses go beyond what the headers state. First, the reference-call test exercises only the span parser. It never feeds the comparison a drifted call, so a comparison that reported nothing would stay green (R05-1). Second, the derived refusal scan counts a message as registered when any registered phrase from any file appears inside it. The register holds phrases as short as twelve characters, so coverage leaks across unrelated refusals (R05-2).

Two more concerns hold as designed. The generated SQL predicates are constants built from the checked-in contract, not from arguments (concern TR-3). The parity test's temporary trees are removed even when a case fails, and leak only if the process is killed (concern RL-2).

The rest fall outside R-05, because nothing here runs in the server, opens a store, or publishes a page. Its single writer, the generator, can be interrupted between its two file writes, and the next --check would report that.

§W-01 — Change impact, refresh, revalidation and review brief

§Concern reasoning

Three seeded concerns turned up defects in W-01, all low. Two further defects fall outside any concern.

concern TR-1. Revalidation's write and read boundaries test reported paths by string prefix without rejecting '..', so src/../x passes src/ (W01-3). impact.ts itself is careful: it passes no argument paths to git, parses the diff with -z, and checks existence with ls-tree -- path.

concern CC-3. The review brief is a derived reader that does not select effective state the way the writers define it:

  • Integral findings come from findings.status, not from the resolution state the open-finding predicate exists to unify.
  • Control claims are marked authoritative without a validity check.
  • A git error in its ancestry test makes an expired claim read as valid (W01-4).

concern IF-3 holds by design. W-01 neither marks nor clears file staleness; clear_staleness alone discharges it. Applying impact in two steps closes claims at the first head, and can miss a file renamed in one step and edited in the next.

The other two defects concern guards that weaken on failure:

  • The refresh run's unowned-drift guard reads a failed diff as an empty range (W01-1).
  • The refresh land wrapper records 'landed' after a landing that was refused (W01-2).
  • Prediction aborts outright when one claim's revision cannot be compared (W01-5).

concern EP-1 holds. Each tool writes in one transaction after its refusals, except the refresh drive, which commits per stage on purpose and resumes by deterministic ids.

concern CR-1 is accepted with a stated residue. Preconditions are read outside the writing transaction everywhere, which is safe within one process. Across two processes, nothing prevents three things, all from reading the code: over-dispatch past the concurrency and budget limits, an overwritten cancel, and a claim closed twice.

concern TB-1 holds. Every git call is bounded by the shared wrapper.

§D-02 — Store gates, rebuild, docs promotion and reader measures

§Calibrating server concerns to one-shot scripts

Most of the checklist was written for a long-lived server that several agent sessions share, and D-02 holds no such process: every script runs once, from a command line or a gate, and exits. Concerns about module state, busy handlers, per-request connections, migration, the code index and record escaping were therefore judged out of scope, each against the reading that shows the script does not touch the thing the probe names.

Where a concern did reach these scripts, the question was whether a failure is visible and recoverable by the operator who started it. That is why concern TB-1 is acceptable here although none of the git, lsof, python3 or stop-and-wait subprocesses has a time limit (dev/promote-docs.mjs:readback@ec39380): a hang is an interruptible command, not a stuck server. The same reasoning covers concern CR-1 (the lsof check and the deletion in dev/rebuild-store.mjs:holdersOf@ec39380 are a check-then-act, refused whenever lsof cannot answer cleanly) and concern EP-1 (a carry refused after the discard leaves an unfinished carry run, but the whole old store is in the printed archive).

The two bugs are the places where the script says one thing and does a weaker one with no operator in the loop to notice. Clause 6 of the completeness checker reads whichever verification run is newest (dev/check-store-fully-surveyed.mjs:verified@ec39380), and the server records one for every materialize_docs and verify_materialized_docs call whatever its mode or directory (mcp-server/src/tools/materialize.ts:execute@ec39380), so the clause is not the clean-export check its title names, and no test drives it. measure-locus-default leaves a copy of the whole store in the temp directory on a narrow failure path, although its own report has a field whose purpose is to say the copy was removed (dev/measure-locus-default.mjs:copyStore@ec39380). A third candidate, rebuild-store's constant marker_validates, was dropped once the server's per-call marker validation was read.

concern SI-2 and concern CC-2 were judged at the level the probes ask for: the checker restates the server's digests and its sorting matcher, the restatements agree at the anchor, and Gate SC5 checks the matcher against the server's and drives the standing reds for rule, sorting, exclusion and ledger writes.

§W-06 — Legacy import, carried findings and store comparison

§Concern reasoning

W-06 owns no infrastructure, so most concern territories reach it only through other subsystems' code. Those were judged where the code lives: storage commits, reconciliation, the code index, publication, the installer and HTML escaping. The concerns that bite are the ones about its own writes and the two databases compare_conspectuses opens.

Resource lifecycle produced the one confirmed defect, W06-1. compare opens path_b before entering the try that closes both handles, so a missing path_b, which the tool's own test drives, leaves path_a's read-only connection open. The leak is small and pins no WAL checkpoint, but the server is long-lived. Temporary directories in W-06's scripts are removed on success and on most failures. The two large test drivers remove theirs as their last statement rather than in a finally; this was judged acceptable.

Atomicity of writes holds. The two multi-row writers, carry_finding and import_artifact_bodies, each commit in one transaction after all their checks and any child process. Concurrency across server processes is held by the schema where it matters most: the carried pair, the outcome chain and the imported path are all unique. What the schema does not bound, rows per carry run and duplicate profile or purpose rows, ends as a refusal at finish_carry_run or as an append-only newest-wins row, not as silent corruption.

Seam contracts with the materializer agree on meaning: withdrawn imports are skipped, and any carry run counts as 'a carry ran'. The imported project purpose passes the materializer's thesis rule but bypasses the server's write-time lint, which is acceptable only because the materializer is the reader that would withhold it.

Trust boundaries are deliberate. The import contains its paths in storage, while compare reads any absolute path read-only, as its description says. All SQL is fixed text with bound values.

§M-02 — Page renderers

§Concern reasoning

M-02 is a read-only Python renderer. Concerns about writes, sidecars, child processes, host configuration and the code index do not reach it, and each of those dispositions names the subsystem that owns the matter.

The concerns that do reach it are about reading and presenting.

  • concern CC-3 (effective rows). Claims, finding states, narratives and explanations are read the way the writers define them. The open-finding count is the exception: the master plan uses a narrower predicate than the subsystem page and the Unresolved lens, recorded as M02-1.

§W-02 — Review sessions, review analysis and composition

§concern CR-1 and concern EP-1: status checks outside the write

Every W-02 handler reads a run, pass or item status and then writes with an UPDATE keyed only on the id, for example land_composition_item (mcp-server/src/tools/composition.ts:landItem@ec393801fd8140a8a9269d3e7132733c4bcb63df). Within one server process the calls are synchronous, so nothing interleaves. Across processes the read can go stale, and the question was what a second writer does. The schema answers it: composition item dispatch, landing and scoring are write-once triggers, run status is a monotonic-status trigger, review pass input is write-once, and completions, exports and reveals are keyed by their session or run (schema.sql 3042-3053, 3331-3403, 2956-2958). A second landing or scoring aborts instead of overwriting. That is why concern CR-1 is acceptable rather than a bug; the residue is a raw SQLite message where a ToolError would be clearer.

For concern EP-1 the multi-row writers were checked one by one: both plans, the two dispatches, land, freeze, aggregate, integral dispatch and scoring, reconcile, compile and complete write in one transaction after their refusals. Three exceptions were weighed. Dispatch-time contamination writes its event and then throws, on purpose, so the event survives the refusal. Reveal writes canary events, a status flip and the reveal row as separate statements, but every refusal (status, already revealed, seal) comes first, and the reveal insert can then fail only to a concurrent reveal. Export writes its two files before its rows; a failing insert (an export_id reused by another session) leaves files with no row, which a retry overwrites. None leaves a partial record that claims more than happened.

§W-03 — Decisions, design sessions and codebase brief

§Concern reasoning

Most of W-03 is well defended against the seeded concerns.

  • It spawns nothing and reads no environment.
  • It keeps no module state.
  • Its SQL is fixed text.
  • Its only path inputs pass the shared survey-scope guards.
  • Every multi-row writer runs its refusals before one transaction. A second process is refused by keys and triggers, though as a raw constraint error.

The weight falls on two concerns, concern CC-3 and concern SE-2, both about what a stored status or a contract sentence says compared with what the code establishes.

concern CC-3: decision authority has two representations, the decision's current-revision pointer and each revision's status. The pointer is maintained correctly. Status is not: accepting a revision supersedes only an accepted direct predecessor. The reconsideration path the tools prescribe (reject, then draft a successor of the rejected revision) leaves the earlier accepted revision accepted. Impact detection selects on status, so it treats that revision as live (W03-1).

concern SE-2: invalidate's description promises an applied impact run, which the code never checks. reject records an authority scope nothing compares (W03-2). The brief's validation row and the development guide imply a JSON Schema check that only the tests perform (W03-3).

The remaining concerns belong to the store, publication, code index and installer subsystems.

§M-06 — Orientation exposure

§Concern reasoning

M-06 is test code that runs single-threaded on throwaway stores, so most of the seeded concerns, which probe the server's handlers, sidecars, installer and shared stores, have nothing to grip here. Two apply. Resource lifecycle holds: every gate removes its temporary store on failure as well as success, through a TemporaryDirectory context manager or, in the survey-notes gate, rmtree in a finally block. Temporal bounds hold only loosely: the gates run the materializer through subprocess.run with no timeout, so a hung render hangs the gate until the CI job's own limit, which is acceptable for test code but turns a hang into a slow failure rather than a red line.

The schema seam is touched but not tested in the probe's sense. The gates execute schema.sql, so a missing table or view would turn them red, but they insert fixture rows directly, so they never show that the server writes what the materializer reads.

The defects that matter here are about the gates' own honesty, and no seeded concern code names them, so they are recorded as findings. The exposure helper has no red case and misses class, stylesheet and details hiding. Three docstrings promise checks the code does not make.

§W-04 — Research, crosswalk and learning ledger

§Concern reasoning

W-04 is server tool code, so the concerns about handlers apply directly.

  • Exceptional paths hold. Every call that writes more than one row does it in one transaction, and the writes outside a transaction are single statements.
  • Concurrency holds within a process. Status checks run before each transaction, and against a second process the schema's state triggers and keys refuse the late writer, with a raw SQLite error.
  • SQL identifiers are interpolated only from constant maps keyed by validated enums.
  • The modules hold no module-level state and start no subprocesses.
  • Scope is enforced through the shared guards: excluded-path evidence is refused at research proposal and on crosswalk evidence sources.
  • Paths cross the trust boundary in two places. Research workspaces and artifacts are guarded against traversal, symlinks and temporary storage. Crosswalk qualification artifacts may be any absolute file on disk, which the server hashes. That is deliberate, but the temp check is narrower than the comment implies.

Cache coherence is the confirmed defect. W-04 reads other subsystems' records by id without applying their own rules about what is current. A rejected decision can receive research, a closed claim can source a crosswalk entity, and the learning ledger and the policy tool disagree about which policy is active.

The other defects concern each module's own logic rather than a seeded concern:

  • learning's preactivation read-back compares a value with itself;
  • a failed lesson and a deferred research request have no way forward;
  • crosswalk counterevidence can never be resolved.

§M-08 — Lens golden pages

§Concern reasoning

M-08 is a test gate plus committed fixture data. Most concern territories describe the server or the published pages that this gate observes, so they are out of scope here. The gate bypasses the tool handlers and never touches a shared store, a code index or a host configuration.

Derived-record drift (concern CC-3) is the one defect. It was framed as: does every committed lens file have a writer that keeps it current, and a reader that would notice if it went stale?

  • Writers: the html and memory.sql are rewritten by a full make-golden.py run, and the html also by --recorded, except the two workspace-dependent pages (materializer/make-golden.py:reprint_recorded@ec393801, evidence 3033).
  • Readers: test-store-only-model.py, test-store-only-no-markdown.py and the convert tests each skip one or both of those pages (evidence 2906, 3045, 3038).
  • md/: no writer and no reader. Its how-to-read page already disagrees with the html on what excluded means (evidence 3069, 3070).

The evidence is code-verified throughout. The finding is LOW because nothing published depends on these files.

Confirmed-acceptable judgments, with the compensating mechanism each rests on:

  • concern AO-1: make-golden.py rebinds CHECKED_SHA on a module instance of its own (evidence 3067).
  • concern EP-2 and concern CC-2: a failed publish or a reconciliation that no longer stands reaches the first page check as a non-ok summary (evidence 3060).
  • concern RL-2: one finally block removes the temp root (evidence 3072).
  • concern TB-1: the subprocesses are untimed, but CI runs the gate as one step whose job limit bounds a hang (evidence 3068).
  • concern IF-2: the committed dump freezes its schema, which turns a schema change into a red comparison, not silent drift (evidence 2882).

concern SE-1 was judged acceptable but worth stating. The gate tests the materializer's reading of schema.sql, not the server's writing of it, as its own docstring says (evidence 2987). Its obligation count follows OBLIGATION_BEARING_SQL, which includes deferred-with-reason rows, while the file_standing view calls those rows excluded. That disagreement is recorded as a lead for the page owners.

concern TR-1 and concern TR-3 were ruled out. The gate takes no arguments, and its SQL interpolates only module constants (evidence 3071).
